Series::dtype¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

DType Series::dtype() const

What It Does¶

Returns compact metadata describing how each value in the Series is stored.

The returned DType is a small, copyable, allocation-free struct with three public fields:

  • scalar — the ScalarType enum value (Float32, Int64, Bool, Complex64, …)

  • itemsize — bytes occupied by one stored value

  • name — the stable printable name ("float32", "int64", …)

and three category queries:

  • is_floating() — any real floating format (Float16, BFloat16, Float32, Float64, and the compact 8-bit float formats)

  • is_complex() — Complex64 or Complex128

  • is_integral() — any signed or unsigned fixed-width integer (Int8…Int64, UInt8…UInt64) — notably not Bool; see the gotcha below

The dtype describes the whole Series at once — there is no per-element representation to inspect. Series also exposes the three category queries directly as methods (is_floating_point(), is_complex(), is_signed()), which are the more direct spelling when a boolean branch is all you need and dtype()’s other fields are not.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

DType A value-type struct (scalar, itemsize, name, and the three category predicates). Inspecting it never allocates, converts, or copies tensor data — it reads metadata only.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — dtype() returns a plain struct, not a Series.

Examples¶

Example 1. The three fields and the three category queries, across a real, an integer, and a complex dtype.

auto real = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto integer = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::UInt32);
auto complex = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::Complex64);
std::cout << "real:    dtype=" << real.dtype() << " itemsize=" << real.dtype().itemsize
          << " floating=" << real.dtype().is_floating() << "\n";
std::cout << "integer: dtype=" << integer.dtype() << " itemsize=" << integer.dtype().itemsize
          << " integral=" << integer.dtype().is_integral() << "\n";
std::cout << "complex: dtype=" << complex.dtype() << " itemsize=" << complex.dtype().itemsize
          << " complex=" << complex.dtype().is_complex() << "\n";

Output¶

real:    dtype=float32 itemsize=4 floating=true
integer: dtype=uint32 itemsize=4 integral=true
complex: dtype=complex64 itemsize=8 complex=true

std::cout << dtype() prints name directly. Complex64 costs 8 bytes — two packed float32 lanes for the real and imaginary parts.

Example 2. Bool is neither floating, complex, nor integral under this classification — it is its own category.

auto b = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::Bool);
std::cout << "bool: floating=" << b.dtype().is_floating()
          << " complex=" << b.dtype().is_complex()
          << " integral=" << b.dtype().is_integral() << "\n";

Output¶

bool: floating=false complex=false integral=false

A routine that branches on “floating vs. integral” and forgets this will silently mishandle boolean tensors — test dtype == ScalarType::Bool explicitly, or use is_signed() style checks the way the rest of Series does.

Example 3. itemsize scales with precision inside the same category.

auto f16 = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Float16);
auto f32 = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto f64 = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
std::cout << "float16 itemsize=" << f16.dtype().itemsize << "\n";
std::cout << "float32 itemsize=" << f32.dtype().itemsize << "\n";
std::cout << "float64 itemsize=" << f64.dtype().itemsize << "\n";

Output¶

float16 itemsize=2
float32 itemsize=4
float64 itemsize=8

All three are is_floating() == true; only itemsize (and precision) differs. This is what makes numel() * dtype().itemsize the right formula for a byte budget — see numel Example 5.

Example 4. to() changes dtype by producing a new tensor; it never mutates dtype() on the original.

auto x = pluss::series::zeros({2}, pluss::ScalarType::Float32);
auto y = x.to(pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
std::cout << "x dtype=" << x.dtype() << "  (unchanged)\n";
std::cout << "y dtype=" << y.dtype() << "\n";

Output¶

x dtype=float32  (unchanged)
y dtype=int64

dtype() is a read of the current state; converting representation is to’s job, and it is always out-of-place unless you reassign.

Choosing The Right Query¶

Use dtype().scalar (or compare dtype() against another DType) when dispatching on one exact representation. Use a category predicate — is_floating(), is_complex(), is_integral(), or the Series-level is_floating_point() / is_complex() / is_signed() — when several representations are equally acceptable. A routine meant to accept “any floating input” should not enumerate Float32 and Float64 by hand and miss Float16, BFloat16, or the 8-bit float formats.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • itemsize is bytes per value, not the tensor’s total storage size. Multiply by numel for that.

  • is_integral() excludes Bool — a boolean tensor is is_floating() == false, is_complex() == false, and is_integral() == false all at once. See Example 2.

  • Complex dtypes report is_complex() == true but are not classified as floating-point, even though their components are floats. Check is_complex() separately whenever both real and complex inputs are accepted.

  • Inspecting dtype() never converts or copies tensor data — only to() does that.

Summary¶

dtype() returns a Series’ storage metadata as a small DType struct:

  • scalar, itemsize, name, plus is_floating() / is_complex() / is_integral() category queries

  • Bool belongs to none of the three categories

  • read-only and allocation-free; to() is what actually converts

  • the Series-level is_floating_point() / is_complex() / is_signed() are the direct spelling for a plain boolean branch

See Also¶

  • Series::is_floating_point, Series::is_complex, Series::is_signed: the direct Series-level category predicates.

  • Series::to: convert a Series to a different dtype.

  • Series::numel: pair with dtype().itemsize for a total byte count.
